How a LiDAR scan becomes a mesh you can ray trace

Every step of bodyscan's static pipeline as a live simulation on real data from one scan (run tt9, fused as pepito). Move the sliders: the algorithms run in your browser with the same rules and default parameters as the package, on 2D slices of the real data, so you can see why each parameter has the effect it has.

2D slices make the mechanisms visible; the package works in 3D, so the numbers here illustrate the trends, not the package's measured results (those are in tuning.md). Technical reference: algorithms.md.

1 · Find the personbackground subtraction 2 · Platform angleICP about the axis, motor model 3 · Fuse the viewssupport, voxels, median surface 4 · Points → surfacePoisson, marching squares 5 · Closed meshsigned distance, ray parity 6 · Smoothbilateral normals, rays

1 · Finding the person: background subtraction

scene.background, scene.isolation · parameters bg_threshold, bg_relative, radius, edge_jump

Every frame is a 128 × 2048 range image. Before the scan the sensor records the empty room for 3 s; its per-pixel median range is the background. In a frame of the scan, a beam is foreground when it returns closer than the background by more than a margin that grows with the distance, because the range noise does:

foreground ⇔ r_background − r > max(bg_threshold, bg_relative · r)

Below: one real beam row of the sensor (all 2048 azimuths, seen from above), recorded with Giuseppe on the platform. Grey: the background. The noise of each beam is measured from the 30 empty-room frames.

drag to pan · wheel to zoom

Controls

beam noise, median
backgroundpersonfalse alarmmixed pixel

Set bg_threshold to 0: noise alone makes beams all over the room "foreground". The relative term keeps far walls (larger noise) quiet while the threshold near the platform stays small enough to keep the feet.

Mixed pixels

A beam is 5 mm wide at the window and diverges 0.35°; where it grazes the edge of the body, part of it hits the body and part the wall, and the sensor reports a range in between. Those points float in the air behind the silhouette. A pixel whose range jumps by more than edge_jump towards both neighbours (horizontally or vertically) is dropped. Then only the largest cluster (DBSCAN, cluster_eps) inside the region is kept.

2 · The platform angle of every frame

registration.icp_turn_about, motion.pairs, motion.models, motion.fitting

To fuse the views, every frame needs the angle the platform had when it was recorded, to about a degree. The motor is not trusted alone (it loses steps under load, and the MATLAB timer starts it by hand), and the images alone are ambiguous. fuse combines both: registrations of pairs of frames give measured turns, and a model of the stepper motor ties them together.

3 · From 378 views to one point cloud

fusion.views, fusion.surface · parameters min_views, support_radius, voxel, confidence_radius

A horizontal slice of the chest (z = 1.30 m above the platform) through all 378 views of the scan. Each view is the person cloud of one frame, turned back by its platform angle about the axis. Stacked, they form a thick, noisy band: range noise (±1 to 4 cm per point in the datasheet), breathing, small sways. The fusion turns that band into one surface in four steps.

drag to pan · wheel to zoom

4 · From points to a surface: Poisson reconstruction

meshing.reconstruct (screened Poisson, Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013) · parameter depth

The points carry normals pointing out of the body. Poisson reconstruction looks for an indicator function χ (1 inside, 0 outside) whose gradient matches the inward normal field V: ∇χ ≈ V (χ grows when you step into the body). Taking the divergence of both sides gives a Poisson equation, solved on an octree:

Δχ = ∇·V   →   surface = { χ = mean of χ at the points }

Below the same equation is solved in 2D on a slice at arm height (z = 1.10 m: torso and both arms), on a regular grid of 2depth cells across the slice, by Gauss-Seidel relaxation from coarse to fine. The contour is extracted by marching squares, the 2D version of marching cubes.

drag to pan · wheel to zoom

Controls

depth (grid 2d across 0.8 m)
points used
cell size
contours
solver sweeps
point → contour, median

Low depth: cells of 5 cm, the arms melt into the torso. High depth: the contour follows every point, noise included. The package uses depth 9 in 3D, cells of about 4 mm on a person; in this 2D slice depth 7 gives 6 mm cells.

Marching squares in one picture

Each grid corner is inside (χ above the iso value) or outside. A cell with corners of both kinds is crossed by the surface; its 16 possible corner patterns select which edges the contour crosses, and the crossing point on an edge is interpolated linearly between the two corner values. In 3D, marching cubes does the same with 256 patterns per cube. Turn on grid to see the cells and the inside corners.

Why the result is closed

χ is defined everywhere on the grid, so its iso-contour cannot have loose ends: every contour closes (or leaves the grid). Where the cloud has a hole, Poisson bridges it smoothly, which is what you want for the soles and the top of the head. Other methods (ball pivoting, alpha shapes) leave holes there.

5 · A guaranteed closed mesh: signed distance and marching cubes

meshing.watertight, meshing.marching · parameter watertight (grid, default 4 mm)

The Poisson surface can still have small defects (doubled sheets, non-manifold edges). The watertight remesh rebuilds it from scratch: a signed distance field on a regular grid (distance to the nearest triangle; negative inside), then marching cubes at level 0. The sign is the delicate part: a point is inside if a ray from it crosses the surface an odd number of times (majority of 5 rays in the package). Click anywhere in the picture to cast a ray.

click: cast a ray · drag: pan · wheel: zoom

Controls

watertight grid
gap between arm and torso
closed contours
gap / grid
ray crossings
verdict

Narrow the gap or coarsen the grid: when the gap falls to about one grid cell the arm fuses with the torso (no grid corner between them is outside). In 3D the package seals gaps narrower than about 1.5 voxels. That is why 4 mm keeps a thumb gap of 30 mm but not fingers 5 mm apart.

The input here is the contour of the real Poisson mesh at z = 1.10 m (the package's pepito_mesh5), with the left arm moved sideways by the slider to set the gap. Every contour that marching squares extracts is closed by construction, edges are shared by exactly two segments, and the orientation follows the sign of the field: closed, manifold and consistently oriented, which is what Sionna RT (Mitsuba) needs.

6 · Smoothing for the ray tracer

meshing.smoothing, bodyscan smooth · parameters scale_mm, rounds, normal_sigma, finish_rounds, finish_scale_mm, keep_volume, max_deviation_mm

A ray tracer reflects every ray on the plane of the triangle it hits. A face of edge L whose vertices have independent errors σ along the normal is tilted by about √2 σ / L radians, and the reflected ray turns by twice the tilt: 0.5 mm of noise on 3.6 mm faces is 11° of tilt and 22° of ray error. The mesh straight from mesh carries the scan rows of the LiDAR as horizontal stripes about 3 cm apart.

Below: the real profile of the pepito mesh, cut by the vertical plane through the body (side view: back on the left, chest on the right). Parallel rays come from the sensor side; watch where they go after the reflection. One round of smooth:

1. bilateral normal filtering (Zheng et al. 2011): every facet normal becomes the average of the normals of the facets within 2 × scale_mm, weighted by length (area in 3D), by a Gaussian of the distance (σ = scale_mm) and by a Gaussian of the normal difference (σ = normal_sigma); 2. vertex update (Sun et al. 2007): the vertices move so that the facets agree with the filtered normals; 3. volume restoration: a uniform offset along the vertex normals restores the area (volume in 3D).

Try scale_mm 6: the small noise goes, the stripes stay. 12 mm removes the stripes. At 24 mm with many rounds the chest and the face flatten and the surface moves several mm. normal_sigma 0.35 keeps creases (chin, armpit) sharp.

What the numbers mean

Facet tilt is the angle between each facet's normal and the mean normal of its neighbours within 10 mm: the random part of the orientation, near 0 on a smooth surface whatever its curvature. It is what the package reports as facet normal noise. Ray error is twice that tilt, the deviation of a reflected ray. Moved is how far the vertices went from the input: the price of smoothing. Read the 90th percentile and the maximum together with the median.

k rounds at σ act roughly like one round at σ·√k; above about 16 mm more smoothing raises the tail of bad facets again. Full table and the effect of every parameter: tuning.md.
